participant.bigIdea: Every organisation that employs BAs already has a practice — the only question is whether anyone is leading it.
participant.overview:
This opening block sets the frame for two days of practice leadership. We separate the **BA practice** (how analysis is actually done across the organisation, defined or not) from the **BACOE** (a small, permanent function that institutionalises and governs that practice). Most of you lead a practice; few of you yet lead a BACOE — and that is fine.

You will lock in the practice you are going to work on for both days and meet the running worked example: the claims-transformation BA practice at Harbourline Insurance, a fictional general insurer, working on *Faster claim settlement for home and motor customers*. Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.
objectives: Distinguish a BA practice from a BACOE in one sentence each
Name the practice you will work on across both days and its current sponsor
Describe the course chain from value proposition to a 90-day plan
Set up your AI agent so it can draft against the BAS playbooks

keyPoints.title: Practice ≠ BACOE
keyPoints.body: The practice is the discipline as exercised by every BA. The BACOE is the governance shell that turns it from a lucky individual outcome into a portfolio-wide capability.

keyPoints.title: One chain, two days
keyPoints.body: Day 1 builds the case and the shape of the practice. Day 2 builds the standards, people, measures and a 90-day plan you can pitch.

keyPoints.title: You direct, the agent drafts
keyPoints.body: Playbooks are structured specs — inputs, steps, success criteria, outputs. Your agent drafts; you bring the real inputs and the judgement.

sections.heading: Why practice leadership is a different job
sections.body:
Leading a BA practice is not being the best BA in the room. A practitioner improves the initiatives they work on; a practice lead improves *every* initiative the organisation runs, including the ones they will never touch. The BAS Practice Model describes three layers of leverage:

| Layer | Unit of value | Typical return |
|---|---|---|
| Individual leverage | One BA positioned upstream of funding | 10–20× cost of the role |
| Disciplined delivery | One initiative at the right tier | Avoids both paperwork and missed nuance |
| Institutional capability | The whole portfolio | 2–6× BACOE cost, far higher in absolute dollars |

The course moves through all three, but the lens is always the leader's: what must be true across the organisation for good analysis to happen by default rather than by luck.

sections.heading: Meet the worked example
sections.body:
Where an example is needed we use one organisation. In our illustrative case, Harbourline Insurance's claims operations team is pursuing **Faster claim settlement for home and motor customers**: notification-to-settlement currently averages **21.6 days**, and the target is **≤10 days within 12 months**, with claim-status calls down 35% — without letting fraud leakage rise.

The BA practice supporting this work is typical of many regulated financial-services practices: capable BAs, mostly engaged after funding is approved, no shared standard for when a Project Vision is required, and no regular value report to the executive. Across both days you will look at this practice through the leader's eyes — what would have to change for its BAs to have shaped the investment rather than documented it?

For contrast, we will also drop in short examples from other sectors — a hospital network, a state government agency, a fintech payments squad, a university — so you can test each idea outside insurance.

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

sections.heading: How the two days fit together
sections.body:
The course follows the book's three layers — individual leverage (Chapter 1), disciplined delivery (Chapter 2) and institutional capability (Chapter 3) — and runs the companion playbooks as you go.

- **Day 1 · Leading the practice** — the value proposition (Ch 1), the Practice Model: four jobs, roles and services and BACOE readiness (Ch 3), boundaries and governance (Ch 3), and the operating layer: the twelve playbooks and the Visual Library. It closes with a three-layer check on your own practice.
- **Day 2 · Growing the practice** — foundations, tiers and templates (Ch 2), roles and career paths (Ch 3), the three value mechanisms (Ch 3), a 90-day Readiness-phase plan, and a five-part executive business case you pitch for feedback.

Each module leaves a saved artefact in this portal. By 16:15 on Day 2 those artefacts become the inputs to your plan. The book's templates and worked examples are in **Downloads**.

modules.title: The BA value proposition
modules.subtitle: Same role, different position, wildly different return

participant.bigIdea: The return on a BA is set by where they sit relative to the funding decision, not by how well they write requirements.
participant.overview:
Most BA practices are positioned as delivery support. They improve clarity and efficiency, and they return roughly **1–3× their cost**. The same skills, positioned *upstream* of funding decisions, return **10–20×** — because they shape what gets funded, not just how it gets delivered.

This module gives you the value theory (the Sammy Value Model), the economics, the conditions under which the high return collapses, and the language you need to make the case to a sponsor without overclaiming.
objectives: Explain value using the Sammy Value Model (Person, Thing, Context, Value)
Contrast delivery-support and investment-shaping BA on the six structural axes
Reproduce the conservative 7.5× base case and explain how it reaches 10–20×
Name the conditions under which the high return will not materialise
Rewrite one position-description responsibility as a Job To Be Done with a value metric

keyPoints.title: Value is an interaction
keyPoints.body: A solution has no inherent value. Value exists only where a specific person interacts with a thing in a specific context.

keyPoints.title: Position sets the ceiling
keyPoints.body: After funding, even exceptional analysis optimises inside a fixed envelope. Before funding, analysis changes the envelope.

keyPoints.title: The when matters too
keyPoints.body: Early analysis changes what is funded; mid-delivery analysis changes the design; late analysis only corrects individual decisions.

keyPoints.title: Contingent, not guaranteed
keyPoints.body: 10–20× needs upstream access, a big enough portfolio, outcome measures, a sponsor who can stop work, and senior judgement.

keyPoints.title: Halve the attribution
keyPoints.body: BAs rarely create value alone. When in doubt, halve the share you claim — credibility is the asset.

sections.heading: A value theory you can defend
sections.body:
Value is spoken about loosely in most organisations. The **Sammy Value Model** (Julian Sammy) makes it precise: value exists only at the intersection of four elements — **Person** (who experiences the benefit), **Thing** (the product, service, process or system), **Context** (the circumstances of the interaction) and **Value** (the perceived benefit). Change the person or the context and the value can change dramatically or disappear.

This is why BAs do not create value by producing artefacts. They create it by deliberately shaping the interaction between people, solutions and context — by surfacing impacts, expanding the organisation's understanding of what must change, aligning tactical execution with strategic intent, and uncovering the dependencies that decide feasibility.

In the worked example, Harbourline's new digital claims portal (Thing) has no value in itself. It has value when a policyholder whose car has been damaged (Person) can lodge with photos and get a desktop assessment straight away, instead of waiting for an external assessor to visit (Context), and is settled in days rather than weeks (Value). The insight that unlocked the outcome was contextual: the assessor-report handoff was being used as a default wait on every claim, however small. The same lens works elsewhere — a hospital's telehealth platform has no value to a rural patient until the referral pathway lets them book it.

sections.heading: Delivery support versus investment shaping
sections.body:
The difference is structural, not a matter of better documentation. It shows up on six axes that travel together:

| Axis | Delivery-support BA | Investment-shaping BA |
|---|---|---|
| Position | Enters after funding is approved | Enters before |
| Mandate | Make a defined initiative succeed | Ensure the right initiatives are chosen |
| Counterparty | Delivery management | Executive sponsor and finance |
| Decision authority | Recommends within scope | Challenges scope — including stop |
| Accountability | Delivery artefacts | Benefits integrity |
| Capability profile | Requirements, modelling, facilitation | Plus commercial judgement and seniority |

The six move together. Putting a delivery-focused BA into an upstream seat without changing mandate, counterparty and accountability produces a frustrated analyst with the wrong job description. As a leader, your job is to change the configuration, not just the person.

![Figure 1.1 — Where the Business Analyst Operates Determines the Return](/files/ba-leadership/Fig_1-1_Where_the_BA_Operates.png)

*Figure 1.1 — Where the Business Analyst Operates Determines the Return — from the book.*

sections.heading: The economics — and how to read them honestly
sections.body:
Take a BA on AUD $150,000, fully loaded at about **$180,000**, influencing a $10–30 million portfolio. Conservative annual contributions:

| Mechanism | Annual value |
|---|---|
| Avoided or reshaped low-value investment | $450,000 |
| Pre-delivery scope optimisation | $250,000 |
| Benefits integrity and capital redirection | $400,000 |
| Structural operational efficiency | $250,000 |
| **Total** | **$1,350,000 (≈7.5×)** |

One material upstream intervention a year — reshaping a $2–5 million initiative — lifts this into the 10–15× band; on $30–100 million portfolios with several such decisions, 15–20×.

Read these numbers with four disciplines. Separate **cashable savings**, **avoided cost** and **value protection** — most BA value is the latter two. **Attribute conservatively** — halve it when in doubt. Treat it as a **decision-quality model**, not a guarantee. And **validate at home** with three pieces of evidence: investments in the last 24 months that missed their benefits, cases where a senior BA changed scope or stopped work, and rework rates with versus without senior BA engagement.

sections.heading: When the return collapses to 1–3×

activities.instructions: Open a real BA position description from your practice. Count the responsibilities that use activity verbs (elicit, document, support, assist) versus decision or outcome verbs (shape, challenge, quantify, stop). Then rewrite the **two** most important responsibilities as Jobs To Be Done, each with a primary metric and a conservative annual dollar value with its assumption stated. Use the worked example if you have no PD.

quiz.q: Why does delivery-focused business analysis cap the return at around 1–3×?
opts: The largest financial decisions have already been made before they arrive
Delivery work has no measurable outcomes
quiz.why: Once capital, scope and assumed benefits are committed, analysis can only optimise inside a fixed envelope. The cap is positional, not personal.

quiz.q: Which is the defining mark of the investment-shaping role?
opts: The recommendation to stop or fundamentally reshape an initiative
quiz.why: Challenging scope — including stopping work — is what the delivery-support role structurally cannot do.

quiz.q: A BA's intervention 'prevented $2m of rework that would have occurred next year'. How should this be classified?
quiz.why: It prevents future spend but does not reduce the current budget — avoided cost. Present it separately from cashable savings.

The six axes move together — change the configuration, not just the person
Claim conservatively and validate with your own portfolio evidence
Name the collapse conditions before a sponsor does

beats.notes: Play the persona; drop the curveball; ask the room for the BA move.

beats.notes: Agent drafts via the aiPrompt; participant challenges every number. Visit breakouts at minutes 5 and 15.

beats.notes: Pairs swap JTBDs. Test: would a CFO accept the assumption? Is attribution halved?

beats.notes: Use the debrief questions; close on the collapse conditions.

presenter.facilitationNotes: This is the module that earns the room's attention for two days — keep the economics crisp and honest. Do not let anyone leave believing 10–20× is a default; say “contingent” at least three times. During BUILD, the most common agent error is inflated dollar values with no assumption: ask “what would the CFO say?” and make them halve it. If a participant's practice is under $5m portfolio, say so kindly and redirect them to the delivery-quality value (rework) rather than investment shaping.

roleplay.persona: The Activity Sponsor — a General Manager who funds the BA team
roleplay.line: “I just need someone who can write good requirements quickly. Why would I pay for a BA to sit in funding conversations?”
roleplay.curveball: Hands over the PD: every responsibility is a delivery verb — elicit, document, support, assist.
roleplay.move: Reframe responsibilities as Jobs To Be Done — decisions, outcomes, risk reduction — and quantify one conservatively, naming the condition it depends on.

presenter.whatGood: Two JTBDs per participant, each with a metric, a conservative dollar value, a visible assumption and halved attribution where uncertain; each participant can name the collapse condition that applies to them.
presenter.commonFailure: Participants inflate the numbers to make the case — and the fix is to require the assumption in writing and apply the halve-the-attribution rule before peer review.
debrief: Where did the agent reach for activity verbs, and how did you reframe them?
Which JTBD carries the biggest value — and what would have to be true for it to materialise?
If you took this to your sponsor on Monday, what's the first question they'd ask?
presenter.answerKey:
**Model JTBDs (worked example).**

1. *Was:* “Elicit and document requirements for claims system changes.” *JTBD:* “Ensure claims initiatives address the measured cause of settlement delay before funding is approved.” Metric: avoided low-value spend. Value: $300,000/yr — assumes one $1.2m initiative a year is reshaped by 50%, attribution halved.
2. *Was:* “Support testing and implementation.” *JTBD:* “Confirm the benefit claimed at approval (notification-to-settlement ≤10 days, fraud leakage flat) is measured after go-live.” Metric: benefits realised vs claimed. Value: $200,000/yr — assumes 10% of the $2.0m addressable value would otherwise go unmeasured and unrecovered.

**Collapse condition most often true:** engaged after funding. A good answer names the specific forum the BA is absent from (e.g. investment committee).

modules.title: The Practice Model: roles, services, maturity
modules.subtitle: Four jobs, four roles, four services — and an honest read of readiness

participant.bigIdea: Individual capability does not scale. Practice does — but only when its roles, services and preconditions are designed on purpose.
participant.overview:
A high-leverage BA is usually a matter of luck: the right person in the right seat at the right time. When that person leaves, the value leaves. The Practice Model is how you make the leverage institutional.

This module covers the four jobs of a practice (set the standard, develop the people, govern the practice, deliver where leverage is highest), the four roles, the four-service catalogue, the six preconditions for a BACOE, and the fallback ladder when they are not met. You will score your own practice against the preconditions.
objectives: Describe the four jobs a BA practice or BACOE performs
Define the four practice roles and the working staffing ratios
Explain the four-service catalogue and the intake workflow
Assess your practice against the six BACOE preconditions and choose the right model

keyPoints.title: Four jobs
keyPoints.body: Set the standard. Develop the people. Govern the practice. Deliver where leverage is highest.

keyPoints.title: Four roles
keyPoints.body: Practice Lead, Lead BA, Senior BA, Business Analyst — roughly one BA per Senior, each Lead anchoring three to five pairings.

keyPoints.title: Four services
keyPoints.body: Investment shaping, delivery assurance, standards and tooling, capability development. No ad-hoc work outside the catalogue.

keyPoints.title: Six preconditions
keyPoints.body: If three or more are not met, do not establish a BACOE — run a lighter intervention and revisit.

keyPoints.title: A stage, not a defeat
keyPoints.body: A Community of Practice with senior anchors often builds the evidence for the later BACOE case.

sections.heading: The four jobs and the four roles
sections.body:
Whether or not you have a formal BACOE, a well-run practice does four jobs: **set the standard** (methods, artefacts, tiers, quality bar), **develop the people** (training, mentoring, community, career paths), **govern the practice** (assure quality, gate-keep investment cases, report value) and **deliver where leverage is highest** (place senior BAs where investment shaping matters most, rather than spreading them thinly).

The work runs on four roles:

| Role | Accountability | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| BA Practice Lead | The practice and its value | ~40% governance and executive engagement, 30% capability and team, 20% standards and quality, 10% hands-on |
| Lead BA | Gold and complex Silver engagements end-to-end | Owns investment-shaping deliverables to sponsor or board; the person standards are calibrated against |
| Senior BA | Silver and Bronze initiatives, Gold streams | Most day-to-day delivery; mentors BAs placed alongside |
| Business Analyst | Defined parts of the work | Paired with a Senior or Lead; builds the senior pipeline |

A practical ratio is roughly **one Business Analyst per Senior**, with each Lead anchoring three to five of those pairings. A BACOE needs at least **60% of staff at Senior or Lead level** to challenge sponsors credibly.

sections.heading: Services and intake
sections.body:
A practice that accepts any work from anyone becomes a resource pool. The BACOE publishes four services:

1. **Investment shaping** — senior BA placement before funding; Project Vision, business case quality review, benefits validation.
2. **Delivery assurance** — quality review on Silver and Gold initiatives at defined gates, without duplicating PMO governance.
3. **Standards and tooling** — templates, methods, training, requirements tooling.
4. **Capability development** — training, mentoring, accreditation, career pathways.

Intake is four steps: the sponsor submits a **one-page request** (problem, expected investment, business owner, service); the Practice Lead **triages weekly** into Bronze, Silver or Gold; a **Senior BA is assigned within five working days** for Silver and Gold; and engagement starts with a **Project Vision workshop within ten working days**. Initiatives under a threshold (typically $250K–$500K) get Bronze treatment regardless of demand.

In the worked example, *Faster claim settlement* would arrive as a one-page request from Harbourline's Head of Claims — and on the five-factor test it is Silver at minimum, arguably Gold given reach across policyholders, brokers, assessors, repairers and the fraud team. By contrast, a fintech squad's request to add a new card-payment option to an existing wallet app would usually triage to Bronze.

sections.heading: Readiness: the six preconditions
sections.body:
A BACOE returns about **2–6×** across the portfolio — lower in multiple than a single upstream BA, far higher in absolute value. But only if:

1. Senior BAs are placed **upstream of funding** decisions.
2. The executive sponsor has **authority to stop** initiatives.
3. **Benefits ownership** sits with the business, not the project.
4. The BACOE **reports above the PMO**, not into it.
5. At least **60% of staff** are Senior or Lead.
6. Funding is committed for **at least three years** (or staged with explicit metrics for each review point).

**If three or more are not met, do not establish a BACOE.** Establish a Community of Practice, a standards working group or a small number of embedded senior BAs, and revisit. A poorly funded or politically constrained BACOE produces worse outcomes than none at all.

When the ideal reporting line is unavailable, use the fallback ladder: **CFO** (preferred — aligned to capital allocation) → **COO** (only if the mandate covers enterprise performance, not just throughput) → **inside the PMO** (high risk; needs a written investment-quality mandate and an escalation path outside the PMO) → **virtual BACOE / Community of Practice**.

sections.heading: Maturity as a pathway, not a score
sections.body:
Maturity in this model is a pathway rather than a ladder of adjectives. A BACOE is built over roughly **24 months in three phases**, each with a decision gate:

| Phase | Months | Gate question |
|---|---|---|
| Readiness | 0–3 | Three-year funding committed and reporting line confirmed? |
| Pilot | 3–9 | Quantified value on at least three pilots, stable operating model? |
| Scale and embed | 9–24 | Portfolio-level reporting, practice independent of any one person? |

Organisations that compress this below twelve months usually skip Readiness or Pilot and pay for it with a defunding decision in Year 2. Your 90-day plan on Day 2 is, in effect, a Readiness phase — or the lighter intervention that builds towards one.

![Figure 3.1 — The BACOE Phased Implementation Pathway](/files/ba-leadership/Fig_3-1_BACOE_Phased_Pathway.png)

*Figure 3.1 — The BACOE Phased Implementation Pathway — from the book.*

sections.heading: What it looks like in practice: the financial services mutual
sections.body:
The book's first case study (a composite) shows the model at mid-size scale. A regional mutual — $800M revenue, 1,200 staff, $52M change portfolio — had BAs spread across IT, operations and transformation with no shared standards; rework averaged 32% and fewer than half of initiatives tracked benefits. After three failed initiatives worth $9M, the CEO sponsored a BACOE: $6.4M over three years, reporting to the **CFO** because investment quality was the main value driver.

In the pilot, five initiatives ran through Project Vision and tier classification: a $14M core banking upgrade was descoped into three tranches (about $2.1M saved), a $6M data warehouse was paused when its benefits assumptions failed, and a regulatory build cut rework from 35% to 14%. Year-2 value was $6.9M against $2.0M cost — **3.45×** — and four years on the BACOE has outlived the CFO who founded it (4.1×).

Use it to test your own diagnostic: which of the six preconditions did this organisation have on day one, and which did the CEO have to create?

*Figure 3.4 — What a BACOE Costs · small, mid-size and large enterprises — from the book.*

activities.title: Run the readiness diagnostic on your practice
activities.instructions: Score each of the six preconditions for your practice as **Met**, **Partly met** or **Not met**, with one line of evidence each. Count the Not mets. Then choose your model: full BACOE, BACOE inside the PMO with conditions, or a lighter intervention (Community of Practice, standards working group, embedded seniors). Finally, map your current staff to the four roles and calculate your Senior-plus-Lead percentage.

modules.title: Influence and decisions: governance
modules.subtitle: Decision rights, forums and boundaries that let the practice say 'stop'

participant.bigIdea: A practice that can recommend stopping an initiative but cannot make anyone listen is a reporting function, not a governance function.
participant.overview:
Influence in a BA practice is designed, not personal. It comes from three things: clear **boundaries** with the PMO, the CIO/CTO and the transformation office; standing **governance forums** where investment quality is decided; and a **sponsor** with the authority to act on what the practice finds.

This module covers the boundary principles, the three governance forums, decision rights and escalation, and how to influence when you do not yet have formal authority.
objectives: State the boundary between the practice and the PMO, CIO/CTO and transformation office
Describe the three governance forums and what each decides
Draft a decision-rights RACI for a real investment decision
Plan influence for a decision where the practice has no formal authority

keyPoints.title: What and why vs how
keyPoints.body: The PMO owns how work is delivered. The practice owns what and why — problem, scope, benefits integrity, requirements quality.

keyPoints.title: Two claimants = wrong boundary
keyPoints.body: If two functions claim the same activity, the boundary is wrong. Resolve it before launch.

keyPoints.title: Three forums
keyPoints.body: Steering Committee (monthly), Investment Quality Forum (fortnightly), Community of Practice (monthly).

keyPoints.title: Fund, reshape, descope, stop
keyPoints.body: The Investment Quality Forum's four outputs. If 'stop' is never used, the forum is ceremonial.

sections.heading: Boundaries with existing functions
sections.body:
The most common political failure of a BA practice is unclear positioning. Without deliberate boundaries it is seen as either redundant or expansionist — and defunded within two years.

| Function | Owns | The practice owns |
|---|---|---|
| PMO | The *how*: schedules, dependencies, delivery forums, status, risk and issue management | The *what* and *why*: problem definition, scope shaping, benefits integrity, requirements quality |
| CIO/CTO | The technical solution: architecture, platforms, build, integration, security, run | The business problem and the conditions under which value will materialise |
| Transformation office | Large-scale change programmes | Senior BA leadership into those programmes and alignment with enterprise standards; governs BAU change outside them |

The test is simple: **if two functions claim the same activity, the boundary is wrong**. The BAS Boundary Negotiator maps the activity landscape, resolves overlaps with these principles, produces a RACI and escalation paths, and ends in a signed Boundaries Agreement.

sections.heading: The three governance forums
sections.body:
**BACOE Steering Committee — monthly.** Chaired by the executive sponsor; attended by the Practice Lead, PMO Lead, CIO representative and transformation office representative. Reviews portfolio value, escalations, boundary issues and operating-model changes.

**Investment Quality Forum — fortnightly.** Chaired by the Practice Lead; attended by senior BAs and PMO portfolio leads. Reviews initiatives at investment-decision stage and produces one of four recommendations: **fund, reshape, descope or stop**.

**BA Community of Practice — monthly.** Chaired by the Capability Lead; open to all BAs. Knowledge sharing, capability development and standards updates.

Without a formal BACOE you can still run lighter versions: a monthly sponsor one-to-one in place of the Steering Committee, and an investment-quality review slot inside an existing portfolio forum.

sections.heading: Decision rights and escalation
sections.body:
Influence fails most often where decision rights are implicit. For every material decision, write down who is **Accountable**, what evidence they need, and when the decision is required. In the worked example:

| Decision | Accountable | Evidence needed | Required by |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 Single digital claims front door vs separate channels per brand and broker | Chief Digital Officer | Channel volumes, broker integration costs | Week 4 |
| D2 Risk threshold for straight-through settlement | Head of Claims | Share of low-value, low-fraud-score claims; leakage impact | Before Release 3 |
| D3 Assessor panel KPI changes | Assessor Panel Manager | Report turnaround and SLA modelling | Before Release 1 pilot |

The practice's role is to make each decision *decision-ready*: the options framed, the evidence assembled, the trade-offs explicit. Escalation should be pre-agreed — for example, a Practice Lead recommendation to stop that is overruled goes to the Steering Committee with the evidence attached and the decision minuted.

sections.heading: Influence without formal authority
sections.body:
Most practice leads start without stop authority. Influence then comes from three sources you can build deliberately:

- **Evidence** — a Project Vision with a baseline, target and measurement plan is harder to ignore than an opinion. In the worked example, showing that the assessor-report handoff (p95 8.7 days) was the largest leak reframed the conversation from “buy a portal” to “stop sending every claim to an assessor”.
- **Stakeholder positioning** — map influence and interest, and engage early anyone who becomes a blocker when consulted late (in the example, the fraud investigations unit and key broker partners).
- **Cadence** — a predictable rhythm (weekly 30-minute steering for high-influence/high-interest stakeholders, a monthly one-pager for the CFO) builds the track record that later justifies formal authority.

The aim is to earn the precondition, not to work around it.

sections.heading: What authority looks like when it is tested
sections.body:
The book's second case study — a national utility with a $240M portfolio — shows the moment a BACOE's authority becomes real. Analysis of a $45M substation automation programme found 30% of proposed sites had an insufficient business case; the programme was rephased and $13M deferred pending evidence. One programme director had publicly committed to dates the BACOE said were unachievable. The dispute went to the CEO, who backed the BACOE. *Politically expensive — and the event that established the BACOE's real authority.*

The mutual's resistance was quieter: the PMO read the BACOE as duplicate governance. It was resolved by **jointly publishing the boundaries agreement** and structuring the Investment Quality Forum to feed existing portfolio governance rather than override it.

The lesson for your RACI: boundaries are signed *before* launch, and the escalation path for an overruled stop recommendation must end with someone who has authority over the portfolio.

modules.title: The operating layer: playbooks, templates and AI
modules.subtitle: Twelve playbooks, twenty-six templates — run by a BA who directs and an assistant that drafts

participant.bigIdea: The chapters explain the logic; the playbooks produce the outputs. A practice runs on its operating layer, not on its slide decks.
participant.overview:
The book closes by naming its executable layer: twelve companion playbooks and a Visual Library of twenty-six template and worked-example pairs. A reader who wants to act on the book does not need to design their own templates — *the playbooks are the templates.*

This module turns that layer into your practice's standard toolkit. You will map the playbooks to the three workflows, compare your practice's current templates with Part III, and agree how your BAs run playbooks with an AI assistant without handing over the judgement.
objectives: Name the three playbook workflows and when each one is run
Use the Part III Visual Library to set the template standard for each tier
Find the gaps between your practice's current templates and the book's twenty-six
Set practice rules for running a playbook with an AI assistant

keyPoints.title: Three workflows
keyPoints.body: Assess roles for value (1 playbook) · Deliver an initiative at the right depth (6) · Build and operate a BACOE (5).

keyPoints.title: Same structure every time
keyPoints.body: Each playbook has defined inputs, structured steps with success criteria and examples, and defined outputs.

sections.heading: Twelve playbooks, three workflows
sections.body:
| Workflow | Playbooks, in order | Who runs it | Book |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 · Assess your BA roles for value | Business Analyst Value Generator | Practitioner or Practice Lead, on each PD | Ch 1 |
| 2 · Deliver an initiative at the right depth | Project Vision Builder → As-Is To-Be Analyser → Tier Classifier → Bronze, Silver or Gold Delivery Pack | Practitioner, on every initiative | Ch 2 |
| 3 · Build and operate a BACOE | Readiness Diagnostic → Business Case Builder → Boundary Negotiator → Operating Model Designer, then Value Reporting Generator every quarter | Practice Lead | Ch 3 |

In Workflows 2 and 3 each playbook's output is the next one's input. Each playbook is 8–25 pages and is designed to be run by a senior practitioner with an AI assistant, or by a Practice Lead facilitating a working session. As the book says, *the playbooks are not training material; they are operating tools.*

![Figure P2.1 — Companion Playbooks Library](/files/ba-leadership/Fig_P2-1_Companion_Playbooks_Library.png)

*Figure P2.1 — Companion Playbooks Library — from the book.*

sections.heading: The Visual Library is your template standard
sections.body:
Part III contains a template and a worked example for every deliverable named in the tiers: 2 foundations, 4 Bronze, 8 Silver and 12 Gold. The worked examples rotate across nine industries, from retail banking to utilities, to show the pattern holds in any sector.

Use it the way the book says: consult it when you are about to produce a specific artefact. Look at the template for the structure, look at the worked example to calibrate depth, then return to your own work. For a practice lead, Part III answers the question every new BA asks: *what is this artefact actually meant to look like?*

**Downloads:** Foundations, Bronze, Silver and Gold packs, plus each template and worked example on its own.

Two rules from Chapter 2 keep the library from becoming paperwork:

- **Artefacts may be combined.** The tier defines analytical *coverage*, not the number of documents. Twelve Gold areas can be twelve documents, twelve sections in one programme handbook, or twelve structured outputs in Jira/Confluence.
- **Documents are evidence, not substance.** A team with one traceable twenty-page handbook covering all twelve areas has met the Gold standard; a team with twelve elegant documents nobody reads has not.

sections.heading: Running a playbook with an AI assistant
sections.body:
Because each playbook already defines inputs, steps, success criteria and outputs, it works as an assistant's instruction set. The BA brings the real inputs (a position description, a concept paper, process data) and the judgement. The assistant removes the blank page — drafting the Jobs To Be Done list, the Readiness Diagnostic, the Vision, the As-Is/To-Be, the tier classification.

The assistant does not know your organisation. Drafts fail in recognisable ways that the book's own tests catch:

| Failure | Book test that catches it |
|---|---|
| Confident numbers with no source | *When in doubt, halve the attribution* and separate cashable, avoided and protected value (Ch 1) |
| Activity verbs dressed as outcomes | Jobs To Be Done are decisions, outcomes and risk reduction (Ch 1) |
| Measures with no baseline | Every measure needs a baseline, a target and a measurement plan (Ch 2) |
| A To-Be that doesn't answer the As-Is | Stakeholders should see the improvement side by side (Ch 2) |
| A tier chosen to look cheaper | Default up in borderline cases (Ch 2) |

sections.heading: Practice rules for assistant-run playbooks
sections.body:
These rules are BAS practice guidance alongside the book. Agree them with your privacy, security and legal teams:

- **Approved tools only:** enterprise-licensed assistants with data-retention controls; no personal accounts for work content.
- **Classify before you paste:** no customer personal information or commercially sensitive figures in tools that are not approved for them.
- **A named human signs:** the sponsor and business owner sign the Vision; the Lead BA signs the tier; no assistant output goes to an investment forum unreviewed.
- **Record what was drafted:** on Silver and Gold artefacts, note which playbook was run, the inputs given, who reviewed it and what they changed.

modules.title: Exercise: three-layer check and close
modules.subtitle: Test your practice against the book's three layers and place it on the pathway

participant.bigIdea: Each layer compounds the one below it — and they must be built in order: leverage, then discipline, then institution.
participant.overview:
The book closes with one thesis and three layers: individual leverage (Chapter 1), disciplined delivery (Chapter 2) and institutional capability (Chapter 3). *A high-leverage BA without delivery discipline is a brilliant individual whose work cannot be verified or scaled. Disciplined delivery without high-leverage positioning is methodological perfection applied to the wrong initiatives. Institutional capability without either is a function that produces governance ceremony rather than enterprise value.*

This exercise tests your practice against each layer using the book's own evidence, places it on the BACOE pathway, and prepares the first part of tomorrow's executive business case: the Problem.
objectives: Test your practice against the three layers using the book's evidence tests
Place your practice on the phased pathway, or name the fallback model that fits
Write the Problem section of a five-part executive business case

keyPoints.title: Three layers, in order
keyPoints.body: Leverage first, because without it there is nothing to institutionalise. Discipline second. Institution third.

keyPoints.title: Evidence over adjectives
keyPoints.body: Each layer is tested with the book's own evidence: a funding-line position, a signed Vision, a value report.

keyPoints.title: A stage, not a defeat
keyPoints.body: If the preconditions are not met, a Community of Practice or embedded seniors is the right stage, not a failure.

sections.heading: The three-layer check
sections.body:
For each layer, answer the book's test with **Yes / Partly / No** and one line of evidence:

| Layer | Book test | Evidence that counts |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · Individual leverage (Ch 1) | Are senior BAs placed *before* the funding decision, with a mandate to recommend stop, descope or reshape? | A named initiative where a BA changed scope, sequencing or cancellation in the last 24 months |
| 2 · Disciplined delivery (Ch 2) | Does every initiative have a signed Project Vision and an As-Is/To-Be, and is it tiered at intake? | Signed Visions; a tier recorded for each initiative; tier-appropriate artefacts |
| 3 · Institutional capability (Ch 3) | Would the practice survive its best BA leaving? Is value reported quarterly against the three mechanisms? | Published standards and service catalogue; governance forums that meet; a value report |

Then use the three internal evidence checks from Chapter 1: a review of investments approved in the last 24 months that missed their benefits; a sample of initiatives where a senior BA materially changed the outcome; and rework on initiatives with and without senior BA engagement. If you cannot find these, your first job is to collect them.

sections.heading: Where you are on the pathway
sections.body:

modules.title: Standards and playbooks: quality gates
modules.subtitle: Two foundations, three tiers, and gates that calibrate rather than burden

participant.bigIdea: The biggest avoidable failure in business analysis is not capability but calibration — heavy method on small problems, light method on large ones.
participant.overview:
Standards are the first job of a practice. The BAS standard has **two foundations** that apply to every initiative — the **Project Vision** and **As-Is before To-Be** — and **three tiers** (Bronze, Silver, Gold) that scale the depth of delivery to the scale of the problem.

This module covers the standard, the five-factor tier test, and how to set quality gates that a practice lead can actually run without becoming a process tax.
objectives: Describe the six elements of a Project Vision and the baseline/target/measurement-plan test
Explain why As-Is precedes To-Be and the side-by-side test
Classify an initiative using the five-factor tier test
Define three quality gates for your practice

keyPoints.title: Two foundations, always
keyPoints.body: Every initiative gets a Project Vision and an As-Is/To-Be. They vary in depth, never in presence.

keyPoints.title: Three tiers, cumulative
keyPoints.body: Bronze 4 artefacts; Silver 12; Gold 24. Each tier inherits the one below.

keyPoints.title: Default up
keyPoints.body: Misclassification is almost always too light. In borderline cases, default up.

keyPoints.title: Coverage, not document count
keyPoints.body: Documents are evidence of analysis, not the substance. Areas may be combined.

sections.heading: The two foundations
sections.body:
**The Project Vision** proves, on a single page, that the analyst understands the problem. Most initiatives fail in framing, not execution: stakeholders agree on a name and a budget but not on the problem. The Vision has six elements: **Problem**, **Desired Outcome**, **Scope Boundaries**, **Stakeholders**, **Early View of the Solution** and **Measures of Success**. A measure counts only if it has a **baseline**, a **target** and a **measurement plan** — otherwise it is a statement of hope.

In the worked example: baseline 21.6 days notification-to-settlement for home and motor claims; target ≤10 days within 12 months of Release 1; measured from the policyholder's first notice of loss to settlement paid, owned by Harbourline's Head of Claims, with a fraud-leakage watch metric that must not rise.

**As-Is before To-Be.** Initiatives stall when the future is designed before the present is understood. The As-Is is evidence of operational reality — delays, errors, data breaks and workarounds — and it defines the scope of impact. The test: a stakeholder should see the improvement by looking at As-Is and To-Be side by side, from their own vantage point. In the example, the As-Is revealed the assessor-report wait (p95 8.7 days) and 27% rework from incomplete first notice of loss re-keyed into the legacy policy admin system — the two problems the To-Be had to solve.

Templates: [Project Vision template](/files/ba-leadership/A1_Project_Vision_Template.png) · [worked example](/files/ba-leadership/A1_Project_Vision_Worked_Example.png) · [As-Is To-Be Analysis template](/files/ba-leadership/A2_As-Is_To-Be_Analysis_Template.png) · [worked example](/files/ba-leadership/A2_As-Is_To-Be_Analysis_Worked_Example.png).

sections.heading: Bronze, Silver, Gold
sections.body:
| Tier | Typical work | Duration and effort | Artefacts | Approval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bronze** | Dashboards, minor enhancements, single-team workflows | 2–6 weeks; ¼–½ BA | 4: Project Brief, Requirements Summary, Configuration Guide, Handover Package | Operational sign-off |
| **Silver** | Cross-team change, integrations, process redesign | 3–9 months; ½–1 BA | 12: Bronze + Business Case, Stakeholder Analysis, Requirements Specification, As-Is/To-Be Models, Solution Design, Data Contracts, Test Plan, Training and Benefits Tracking | Investment committee |
| **Gold** | Platform replacement, multi-year, regulatory, cross-agency | 12–36 months; 2–5 BAs + lead | 24: Silver + Strategic Business Case, Enterprise Stakeholder Plan, Enterprise As-Is/To-Be, Enterprise Requirements, Solution Architecture, Data Strategy, Roadmap, QA Framework, Change Plan, Operations Handbook, Benefits and Risk | Board |

Bronze is a discipline of restraint; Silver is rigour without ceremony; Gold is a defensible foundation and assurance trail for the largest investments. **Artefacts may be combined** — twelve areas of analysis can live in one well-structured Confluence space.

![Figure 2.1 — BA Deliverables by Project Type](/files/ba-leadership/Fig_2-1_BA_Deliverables_by_Project_Type.png)

*Figure 2.1 — BA Deliverables by Project Type — from the book.*

sections.heading: Choosing the tier
sections.body:
Score five factors as small, medium or large: **Cost** (including five-year run cost), **Risk** (reversible / recoverable / strategic damage), **Reach** (teams, systems, processes, customers), **Reversibility** and **Strategic visibility**. Mostly small → Bronze; mostly medium → Silver; mostly large, **or any two large** → Gold. In borderline cases, **default up** — the bias is always towards lighter, and its cost is paid later by someone else.

Worked example: Cost medium ($6.8m three-year), Risk large (claims payments, fraud exposure and conduct obligations to policyholders), Reach large (policyholders, brokers, assessors, repairers, contact centre), Reversibility medium, Visibility large → **Gold** by the any-two-large rule, even though it might be argued as Silver on cost alone. Contrast a university's enrolment-form redesign: mostly small or medium → Silver at most.

sections.body:

sections.heading: Quality gates a leader can run
sections.body:
Quality gates turn the standard into practice. Keep them few and tied to decisions:

1. **Gate 1 — Vision signed** (all tiers): six elements present, checked against the A.1 template; measures have baseline, target, measurement plan; sponsor and business owner signed. *Before any requirements work.*
2. **Gate 2 — Tier confirmed** (all tiers): five-factor score recorded; As-Is evidenced; To-Be addresses each As-Is pain point (the A.2 side-by-side test). *Before business case or build.*
3. **Gate 3 — Benefits handed over** (Silver and Gold): benefit measure live (C.8 or D.12), business owner accepts ownership. *Before project closure.*

Delivery assurance reviews Silver and Gold at these gates without duplicating PMO stage gates. Bronze is assured by template and spot-check.

These gates are how a practice runs the book's *Delivery assurance* service. They are BAS practice guidance built on the book's tests, not a separate methodology.

modules.subtitle: Build the senior pipeline the practice depends on

participant.bigIdea: A practice without seniors cannot challenge sponsors; a practice without juniors runs hot now and dry later. The ratio is a leadership decision.
participant.overview:
Developing the people is the second job of a practice. Investment shaping requires experience and gravitas that methodology cannot substitute, so the practice lead's capability strategy is really a seniority strategy: how BAs move from delivering defined parts of the work to shaping investment decisions.

This module covers the four roles as a career path, the role-family taxonomy that makes them recognisable outside your organisation, pairing and coaching models, and a capability plan for your practice.
objectives: Describe the career path from Business Analyst to Practice Lead and the shift at each step
Map your practice to the BA role family and identify adjacent families
Design a pairing and coaching model using the working ratios
Run a structured coaching conversation that moves a BA upstream

keyPoints.title: Career path = shift in counterparty
keyPoints.body: BAs work with delivery teams; Seniors with business owners; Leads with sponsors and boards; the Practice Lead with the executive.

keyPoints.title: Recognisable titles
keyPoints.body: The four roles map to the IIBA Career Road Map and Clare's role family, so progression and benchmarking work without translation.

keyPoints.title: 1:1 and 3–5

keyPoints.title: Coach the move, not the template

sections.heading: The four roles as a career path
sections.body:
| Step | Works mainly with | The capability shift |
|---|---|---|
| Business Analyst | Delivery teams, Senior BA | From completing tasks to understanding why the task matters; modelling, elicitation, testing handover |
| Senior BA | Business owners | Owns the outcome of investment decisions on initiatives they shape; mentors a BA; carries organisational knowledge |
| Lead BA | Sponsors, boards | Runs Gold and complex Silver end-to-end; owns investment-shaping deliverables; the person standards are calibrated against |
| Practice Lead | Executive, peers in PMO/CIO/transformation | Owns the practice's value, business case, boundaries and standards |

The defining shift is not technique but **counterparty and accountability** — the same six axes from Day 1. A Senior BA who has never sat with finance is not yet ready to be a Lead, however good their models are.

sections.heading: The role family and adjacent families
sections.body:
The four practice roles map onto the BA role family first published by Clare (2008) and maintained by IIBA as the Business Analyst Career Road Map. Business Analyst and Senior BA sit on the career spine; the Lead BA sits at the transition into the BA leadership family; the Practice Lead sits in that leadership family as the COE leader role, interfacing upward into senior leadership.

The extended family makes adjacent paths explicit — **Product Management, Agile/Delivery, Data and Analytics, UX/Service Design**, as well as project management, testing and business operations. A capability framework should name the legitimate exits and re-entries: a strong BA who moves into product ownership for two years often returns as a better Lead. Retention is about pathways, not just pay.

![Figure 3.2 — The BA Role Family (extended)](/files/ba-leadership/Fig_3-2_BA_Role_Family.png)

*Figure 3.2 — The BA Role Family (extended) — from the book.*

sections.heading: Pairing and coaching models
sections.body:
A practical working ratio is **one Business Analyst per Senior**, with each **Lead anchoring three to five pairings**. Too many Business Analysts relative to Seniors and Leads produces output that looks like analysis but cannot challenge a sponsor, and reduces the mentoring time of the most experienced people. A BACOE needs **at least 60% Senior or Lead** if it is mandated for investment shaping; below that, mandate it for capability development first.

The **Practice Lead's own time** is part of the design. The book's split: roughly **40%** governance and executive engagement, **30%** capability and team leadership, **20%** standards and quality, **10%** hands-on work where strategic visibility needs it.

Development happens through the work:

- **Pairing on live work** — the BA drafts, the Senior reviews and explains the judgement. In the worked example, a BA drafts the As-Is pain-point inventory; the Senior shows why the assessor-report wait matters more than the payment batch run.
- **Lead quality review** — Lead BAs review the work of Seniors and BAs on their initiatives; they are *the people standards are calibrated against*.
- **The Community of Practice** — monthly and open to all BAs: knowledge sharing, capability development, standards updates.
- **Stretch by counterparty** — the next assignment moves a BA closer to the funding decision: observing the Investment Quality Forum, then presenting to it.

sections.heading: Career pathways and what they retain
sections.body:
In Phase 3 the book's pathway includes a capability framework: careers, training and accreditation. The national utility case published three pathways in month sixteen — **delivery BA**, **investment BA** and **practice BA** — and appointed its most influential sceptical seniors as Standards Working Group leads.

The result was not in the original business case: BA attrition to consultancies fell from **18% to 7% a year**, and the utility began attracting senior BAs from competitors. A visible pathway is a retention strategy as well as a capability one.

sections.heading: A capability plan for your practice
sections.body:
A capability plan answers four questions: **What is our seniority mix now and in 12 months?** (target ≥60% Senior/Lead if you intend investment shaping). **Who is paired with whom?** **Which three capabilities matter most?** (commonly commercial judgement, facilitation of difficult decisions, and value quantification). **How will we know it's working?** (e.g. number of BAs who have presented to a sponsor; Visions passing Gate 1 first time).

Rewrite position descriptions as part of the plan: the Value Generator exercise from Day 1 gives you outcome-language PDs for each role, which become both the career framework and the performance conversation.

modules.title: Measuring practice value: KPIs
modules.subtitle: Three mechanisms, staged measures and a report a CFO will read

participant.bigIdea: A practice that cannot show its value will eventually be measured on its cost.
participant.overview:
Value reporting is what turns a practice from an overhead into an investment. The BAS model measures practice value through **three mechanisms** — investment decision quality, delivery efficiency and rework reduction, and benefits integrity — reported quarterly to the Steering Committee and annually to the board.

This module covers the mechanisms, how to build KPIs with a baseline, target and measurement plan, how to stage measures over one versus three years, and how to report value honestly.
objectives: Describe the three value mechanisms and how each is quantified
Build practice KPIs with baseline, target, measurement plan and owner
Stage measures for 90 days, 12 months and three years
Draft the structure of a quarterly value report

keyPoints.title: Three mechanisms
keyPoints.body: Investment decisions reshaped or stopped; rework and delivery efficiency; benefits integrity and capital redirection.

keyPoints.title: Conservative model
keyPoints.body: A $2.0m BACOE on a $60m portfolio: $4.5m annual value, 2.25× — before higher-performing cases reach 4–6×.

keyPoints.title: Stage the metrics
keyPoints.body: Twelve-month metrics differ from three-year metrics. Agree both up front or be judged on cost.

keyPoints.title: Lead and lag
keyPoints.body: Pair each outcome measure with a leading indicator you can move in 90 days.

sections.heading: The three value mechanisms
sections.body:
**Mechanism 1 — Investment decision quality.** Senior BAs before funding reshape, descope or stop initiatives that would consume capital without benefit. On a mid-size portfolio this is typically 3–5% of annual change spend — consistent with PMI's finding that 11.4% of investment is wasted through poor project performance.

**Mechanism 2 — Delivery efficiency and rework.** Standards and assurance reduce rework from 25–40% of project cost to 10–15% in mature practices. Only a portion is practice-attributable.

**Mechanism 3 — Benefits integrity.** 30–50% of claimed benefits are never measured after implementation. A practice that owns benefits tracking turns invisible value into evidenced value.

| Mechanism ($60m portfolio, $2.0m BACOE) | Conservative annual value |
|---|---|
| Investment decisions reshaped or stopped | $1,800,000 |
| Rework and delivery efficiency (attributable) | $1,500,000 |
| Benefits integrity and capital redirection | $1,200,000 |
| **Total** | **$4,500,000 — 2.25×** |

sections.heading: The conservative calculation — and the case studies
sections.body:
The book's conservative model for a mid-size enterprise ($60M portfolio, $2.0M BACOE):

| Mechanism | Conservative annual value |
|---|---|
| Investment decisions reshaped or stopped | $1,800,000 |
| Rework and delivery efficiency (BACOE-attributable share) | $1,500,000 |
| Benefits integrity and capital redirection | $1,200,000 |
| **Total** | **$4,500,000** — net $2.5M, **2.25×** |

The two case studies report Year-2 value the same way, mechanism by mechanism:

| | Mechanism 1 | Mechanism 2 | Mechanism 3 | Total vs cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Financial services mutual | $4.2M | $1.8M | $0.9M | $6.9M vs $2.0M — 3.45× |
| National utility | $14M | $7.2M | $4.8M | $26M vs $4.0M — 6.5× |

Your quarterly value report should use this structure from day one, even when early figures are small. The case-study figures are composites and illustrative ratios, as the book notes.

sections.heading: Building KPIs that survive scrutiny
sections.body:
Each practice KPI needs a **baseline**, a **target**, a **measurement plan** (data, source, cadence, owner) and a statement of **what it doesn't measure**. A useful set covers all three mechanisms plus practice health:

| KPI | Mechanism | Type |
|---|---|---|
| Value of initiatives reshaped, descoped or stopped at investment stage | 1 | Lag |
| % of Silver/Gold initiatives with a senior BA assigned before funding | 1 | Lead |
| Rework as % of delivery cost on BA-assured vs non-assured initiatives | 2 | Lag |
| % of Visions passing Gate 1 first time | 2 | Lead |
| % of claimed benefits with a live measure 6 months after go-live | 3 | Lag |
| % of initiatives with benefits owner accepted at Gate 3 | 3 | Lead |
| Senior + Lead % of practice | Health | Lead |

The worked example shows the pattern at initiative level: the north-star (notification-to-settlement) is supported by tier-2 drivers, each with an owner and source — % claims lodged digitally (CDO, portal analytics), % first notices complete at submission (Head of Claims, claims data warehouse), assessor report turnaround p95 (Assessor Panel Manager) — with fraud leakage as the watch metric. A practice KPI tree works the same way.

sections.heading: Staging measures over time
sections.body:
A practice funded for twelve months and judged at twelve months will be measured on its costs and published templates, not on investment-quality outcomes that take longer to mature. Agree a staged scorecard at the outset:

- **90 days** — leading indicators only: senior BAs placed upstream on named initiatives; Gate 1 in use; value baseline captured.
- **12 months** — first quantified Mechanism 1 and 3 cases on at least three pilots; first quarterly value report delivered.
- **3 years** — portfolio-level value against the three mechanisms; return multiple reported to the board.

In the worked example, an upstream BA on the next Harbourline claims initiative could show a 90-day leading indicator (placed before investment committee) long before the lagging value (avoided spend) is provable. A state government agency redesigning a grants platform faces the same trap in a different form: annual budget cycles judge the practice before any benefit can land.

sections.heading: Reporting value honestly
sections.body:
The BAS Value Reporting Generator aggregates contributions across the three mechanisms, compares actual to target, identifies trends, surfaces risks, and produces either a **quarterly value report** for the Steering Committee or an **annual board report**.

Three honesty rules protect credibility: separate **cashable, avoided and protected** value; **halve attribution** when in doubt and say so; and report **misses** alongside wins — a report with no red is not believed. A one-page quarterly report has four parts: value this quarter by mechanism; leading indicators against target; risks and preconditions at threat; decisions needed from the Steering Committee.

**Model scorecard (worked example practice, illustrative).**

modules.title: Build your 90-day practice plan

participant.bigIdea: Ninety days is a Readiness phase: long enough to prove one thing, short enough that nobody loses interest.
participant.overview:
In the BAS pathway the first phase of building a practice — **Readiness, months 0–3** — confirms preconditions, secures backing, agrees boundaries and builds the case. Your 90-day plan is that phase, or the lighter intervention that builds towards it.

This module assembles everything you have produced — value proposition, readiness diagnostic, boundaries and decision rights, Visual Library coverage map and practice rules, three-layer check, tier and quality gates, capability plan and scorecard — into one plan with three workstreams, a pilot, a decision gate and an ask.

Select one pilot initiative that can evidence a value mechanism
Define the day-90 decision gate and what it unlocks

keyPoints.title: Three workstreams
keyPoints.body: Position (where BAs sit), Standard (gates and playbooks), People and proof (capability and value reporting).

keyPoints.title: One pilot
keyPoints.body: One upstream placement on one initiative beats a programme of templates.

keyPoints.title: A gate at day 90

keyPoints.body: Compressing Readiness is the most common cause of defunding in Year 2.

sections.heading: The shape of the plan
sections.body:
A 90-day plan has five parts:

1. **Starting point** — your three-layer check and pathway position (Day 1 close).
2. **Model choice** — full BACOE track, conditional PMO-hosted model, or lighter intervention (readiness diagnostic).
3. **Three workstreams over three months**:

| Workstream | Days 1–30 | Days 31–60 | Days 61–90 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Position | Agree pilot initiative; senior BA placed upstream | Project Vision signed; tier confirmed | Investment Quality review held on pilot |
| Standard | Gate 1 published with the A.1 Project Vision template; practice rules for assistant-run playbooks agreed with privacy/security | Gate 2 in use; tier template set adopted from Part III | Gate 3 drafted; boundaries discussion with PMO |
| People and proof | Baselines captured; pairings agreed | Community of Practice launched; first coaching cycle | 90-day value report delivered |

4. **Day-90 decision gate** — what you will ask for and the evidence.
5. **Risks and asks** — preconditions at threat and the decisions needed from your sponsor.

If you are on the BACOE track, Phase 1 of the book's pathway names the artefacts your 90 days should produce: **Readiness Diagnostic, capability heat-map, Boundary Negotiator agreement, Business Case Builder output and a funding decision.** If you are on a lighter intervention, the plan builds the evidence that later justifies the business case.

sections.heading: Choosing the pilot
sections.body:
A good pilot initiative is **pre-funding** (so Mechanism 1 is available), **Silver or Gold** (so there is enough at stake), has a **business owner willing to own benefits**, and is **visible to your sponsor**. Avoid initiatives already in delivery — they can only show delivery-band value.

In the worked example, *Faster claim settlement* is already funded, so it is a poor Mechanism 1 pilot. A better choice is the next initiative in Harbourline's pipeline — for example, fraud-detection rules modernisation, which was explicitly out of scope — where a senior BA could join before investment committee and apply the same assessor-wait insight: find the default wait or manual check hidden in the process.

sections.heading: The day-90 gate and the ask
sections.body:
End the plan with the decision you want at day 90 and the evidence that would justify it. Typical gates:

- *Lighter intervention → BACOE readiness:* “Evidence from one pilot and two unmet preconditions now met; approve the BACOE business case build.”
- *Embedded seniors → standard placement:* “Pilot showed value; make senior BA placement before investment committee the default for Silver and Gold.”
- *Standards → governance:* “Gates adopted; establish the fortnightly Investment Quality Forum.”

The ask must be specific, within the sponsor's authority and tied to evidence you will actually have at day 90.

keyPoints.title: Five parts

sections.heading: The pitch structure — the five-part executive business case
sections.body:
| Part | What the book asks for | Pitch time |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · Problem | The cost of the current state: change spend lost to poor investment decisions, rework and unrealised benefits — your own data where possible | 60 s |
| 2 · Proposed Investment | Structure, staffing and cost over three years, including year-one setup and steady state — or the lighter intervention and its cost | 45 s |
| 3 · Expected Return | The three mechanisms, the conservative annual value, the net return, and the preconditions it depends on | 75 s |
| 4 · Risks and Failure Conditions | When it will fail, and the mitigations the sponsor commits to | 45 s |
| 5 · Recommendation | The decision, the funding, the reporting line, the sponsor, the launch date and the first review point | 45 s |

You wrote Part 1 at the end of Day 1, and your scorecard gives you Part 3. For a 90-day Readiness plan, the Recommendation is usually the day-90 gate: the decision you want, and the evidence that will justify it.

The worked-example pitch opens with the Problem: “Our BAs joined *Faster claim settlement* after it was funded — and the biggest leak, an assessor-report wait of up to 8.7 days, was only found in delivery. Imagine finding that before the business case.”

sections.heading: Giving useful feedback
sections.body: Feedback givers play the sponsor and then step out of role to give three lines: **what will land**, **what the sponsor will challenge first**, and **what to cut**. Keep it specific and kind; the goal is a better pitch on Monday, not a perfect one today.

Run the playbooks as you implement: the Readiness Diagnostic before any business case, the Business Case Builder to turn today's pitch into the full document, the Tier Classifier at intake, and the Value Reporting Generator each quarter. Repeat your three-layer check at day 90 and compare.
